video_title: Peter Boockvar: Inflation Is The Core Disease
transcript: Welcome to the Risk Reversal podcast. I am Dan Nathan, that is Guy Adami. >> This is Guy Adami, and I'm so excited. Do you know why, Dan? >> Yeah, cuz of our guest. >> The great Peter Boockvar, who has joined us numerous times, and you know, on the pantheon of guests, he's right up there. He's he's in it, Dan. >> He is in it. So, Peter is the CIO at 1 Point BFG Wealth Partners. Peter, welcome back to the 27th time with Guy and me over the last 5 and 1/2 years. >> I I I love it. I appreciate all the opportunities I get on to to chat with you guys. Uh obviously, there's always something to discuss, and uh it's always one of my favorite parts of the day. >> Oh, well, here's the deal. We got plenty to discuss today. You know, we want to go over some data last week and just maybe try to find some through lines between the inflation data that we saw on Wednesday and Thursday, and then the move, I think, in yields or the lack thereof, and then some of the data that we had on Friday morning, um about consumer confidence and retail sales, and then we're going to look ahead to some of the earnings, the Fed minutes. Um so, lot to talk about. Guy, where do you want to start? >> I think we should start with the inflation data, Peter, which, listen, according to the pundits you listen to or read, a lot of people thought they came in soft, light, better than expected, whatever term you want to use. And you know what? That's fine. I'll give you that. But what's remarkable to me, and I think Dan sort of alluded to it, as we're sitting here, bond market doesn't seem to care all that much. As a matter of fact, I'm shocked by how resilient yields are, how weak the bond market is. So, let's start there. >> Well, the inflation stats, if you include the revision upward in PPI, that was spot-on, as was CPI. I think notable in the yield curve is the 2-year yield has has dipped, while the 10-year yield is is pretty persistent here at 465-ish and change. So, the yield curve is steepen to touch, but in a bear steepener fashion. I think noteworthy within the inflation stats is that PPI is still running well above CPI. When I hear people tell me about their inflation argument and what the Fed should do, they only look at CPI. And I continue to argue that the full picture on inflation must include wholesale prices because somebody has to eat that. And I heard many times both uh at the company level, uh but also in the Fed's Beige Book that we saw in July, was some companies are having success in passing on their higher costs, but others are not. So, if a if a price pressure gets stuck at the producer level, doesn't flow through to consumers, doesn't mean that it disappeared. So, I think the Fed needs to look at both uh in order to make a you know, a better educated inflation outlook, uh which then obviously flows through to rates. >> You know, which is and I'll say this quickly. I mean, that's why you you don't look things you don't look at things on just sort of the surface. I mean, you sort of get down two, three uh standard deviations away. And and I just want to sort of add this. That's why I think I'll I'll continue to think the Fed is right to sort of continue to sort of target inflation as the problem. >> I I I agree. The one interesting thing that I'm still just trying to figure out here is that inflation break-evens in the TIPS market are where they were before the war even began. And I still think it's it's it's a it's an indicator. I still think that it's a measure of what markets think about inflation, and those expectations are still rather benign. So, either the TIPS market is a screaming buy in in terms of inflation in reality coming in higher than what's currently priced in, which I believe, or uh the Fed is right just to sit and do nothing where current inflation expect uh it current inflation figures are still rather persistent. But Kevin Warsh is looking at the TIPS market and saying, well, market still believes that uh we're still going to actually see a fall in inflation. Kevin Warsh watches the markets more so than any Fed chair that we've had. And I know he's looking at the TIPS market. So, it's this this kind of interesting bifurcation situation uh with one market telling us one thing and some of the stats telling us another. >> So, Peter, given, you know, the data and the breakdown on the inflation front this week, consumer confidence number uh this morning, inflation expectations which you just gave, you know, they're they're not ramping dramatically. Is that a fair um sort of assessment? So, when you think about the Fed chair and watching the markets, and this is something that's been very clear that he's kind of dictated over the last few months, we don't have a Fed meeting uh this month. We go to uh I I think it's September 16th or 17th uh the next meeting. We are going to have inflation data uh CPI and PPI PCE, too. Is that coming up pretty soon? So, as far as, you know, any sort of change in narrative, and I know that's something that Fed chair Warsh doesn't want to do. He's going to be at Jackson Hole what, in 2 weeks or something like that? Oftentimes we've heard some commentary out of a Fed chair that changes the narrative just a little bit. Are the expectations for anything other than just a kind of stay the course and kind of give his two cents by continuing to watch the markets, but in mid uh September? >> I I I think he's going to still sit on his hands. But the Fed is is is reached what I believe is a very interesting situation that's difficult. You know, a lot of Fed watchers, they say, "Okay, the Fed's either going to focus on the inflation side. If it's higher than expected, we'll try to cool that down, or they'll flip to the labor market side." But I I I believe and I argue that inflation is the core disease of the economy right now. And the slowdown in hiring that we've seen in the labor market, even though the pace of hiring is is still really really low, is the symptom of those inflation issues. So, if you look at the consumer, wage growth is still pretty good, but it's moderating to the point where it's growing really no more than the pace of inflation. So, the consumer, the average consumer, is on this hamster wheel. And Dan and Guy, I'll use a quote from a music a song, running to stand still. >> Nice. >> They're not gaining any progress. So, I think that helps to explain why the consumer confidence number is still relatively low. And one line item in the August consumer price index consumer confidence index from the Michigan survey was the percentage of those that believe that their income will exceed inflation over the next 5 years, mean number was the second lowest dating back to my Bloomberg data in 1998. So, that remains the problem. So, well, if labor market starts to weaken, but it's because high inflation, does Kevin Warsh respond to the weaker labor data by cutting rates? Or does he still remain focused on taming inflation, which if he's successful at doing, that will then help the labor market. It is this very difficult situation that a dual mandate situation that the Fed responsibility the Fed has, now it's getting really complicated. If it was just inflation, then he would continue to be tight with money. Now, it's going to be really complicated for him. >> I brought that up on Fast Money at one point about the labor market, the deterioration that I'm seeing in the labor market. I was pushed back on a little bit and obviously, look, the unemployment rate has fallen down to 4.1% but there are extenuating circumstances that can be sort of explained away. But they're going to have to deal with a labor market that I think is sort of turning towards the wrong side of the equation. And again, inflation problems that are a concern. In University of Michigan, you know, we have these conversations with Liz Thomas of SoFi. I mean, that number of 51 was well short of the 54.4. I think Michigan surveys about a 500 or so consumers. And these surveys tend to be very inflation biased. So, to your point, people are absolutely feeling it regardless of what you hear from some of the punditry out there. >> Yeah, and and some of these consumers that are surveyed are business owners as well. And that gets to the point I made earlier is that wholesale inflation, cost pressures at the business level still remains very elevated and not all companies are able to pass it on. And I heard many times uh through a lot of conference calls about further productivity enhancements that companies are employing to mitigate other cost pressures. And one of those happens to be a tighter rein on hiring. Because if you want to maintain your margin and you can't pass on your uh uh your higher costs because the consumer's pushing it back against you, well, you're going to limit the wage increases to your employees and you're also going to limit the pace of hiring, particularly on the small business side. Now, small business hiring went negative last year in response to the tariffs because they were at least able to uh respond to a very sharp rise in their cost structure. Small business hiring has rebounded this year, but I think that in the uh ADP number that we saw for July, we actually we some a bit of softening again. So, that's what I'm going to watch going forward. And again, getting to that point where inflation is everywhere, but some are feeling it more than others. >> So, Peter, um doing some of the data um of late, we saw that big move. Guys detailed that in the 30-year. This was coming back. I think it was after the Fed shares last meeting and some of the commentary there. If you look at crude oil right here, it's trading at 81 and 1/2 WTI. The average of the last 6 months really since the war started is about 87, if you think about that, right? So, if we're going and doing a look back a little bit. So, you have high yields, you have high crude, you have inflation that is not listening to you both. It's just the headline, the fact that it kind of dropped, you know, on a sequential basis um is not particularly um that interesting. Why is it the S&P 500 is just levitates? It had that huge breakout a week and a half ago after being in a fairly tight range. So, investors in the stock market do not seem bothered by anything of what we just talked about for the last 7 minutes. >> Because the the AI capex spend doesn't care whether it wells at 80, 90, or 100. Those dollars are going to flow into all the infrastructure providers to it. And it's not just the direct beneficiaries of the AI spend. You look at the financials. Well, what benefited the money center banks? It was capital markets. It was all uh the the the trading and the and and the capital raises for AI. And look at upper income restaurants. Stock market benefiting from AI. Everything is dependent on AI's buildout and the stock market beneficiaries keeping the S&P uh inflated. It is I don't want to be hyperbolic, but it is an all-in trade both economically and market-related. And we talk about earnings and we hear about earnings are unbelievable and you got to buy stocks is Well, earnings are unbelievable because of all that cap ex spend. What were the biggest drivers of earnings growth? We know it was tech, we know it was communication services, which is also benefiting from that. Uh financials benefiting from AI indirectly, and then of course you have energy, but that was obviously war war related, but economics, stock market, earnings all a derivative of the massive AI cap ex spend. So, while the party is on, things are great, and I'm not smart enough to know when it ends, but people should at least know what we're riding on here to be able to watch for signals that that ride may slow down at some point. Actually, not if it slows down, it's when it slows down at some point. >> All right, let's talk about what we have this week because it's sort of retail week, and I'm not asking you to play stock market here, but more so the importance of these names. Home Depot on Tuesday, Lowe's, Target, TJ Maxx on Wednesday, throw a Walmart in on Thursday, and you have some of the biggest retailers in the world telling us what they saw in the quarter, maybe more importantly what they're seeing going forward. >> I think it's going to be pretty similar in terms of story. Home Depot and Lowe's are going to tell us that their commercial business is okay, but their do-it-yourself and big ticket items are still soft. Uh when when existing home sales are running at 30-year lows, less people do renovation and remodeling because when you have that home turnover, that's when you tend to do more of it. We know that Ross Stores and TJ Maxx and those, you know, value dependent retailers will tell us that business is great because the consumer is value conscious, and those are the the perfect stores for those seeking bargains. Walmart's going to tell us that, you know, business is fine. However, uh you You the low-income consumer may be still more very sensitive to gas prices cuz interestingly enough, the average gallon of gasoline from AAA in the middle of August has never been this high. You know, we're coming to the end of the driving season and typically prices start to drop in anticipation of a falloff after Labor Day. We're not seeing it. And also what what we're going to hear from Walmart and Target is that consumer making more than $100,000 continues to shop at their stores because that sort of middle-income consumer is also searching for bargains as well. >> Is there something of particular focus? Again, we've been talking about the trade down in you know, Walmart it seems like for a couple of years. Last quarter the stock was trading at an [music] all-time high heading into the print and it looked like one of these very defensive names for a whole host of reasons, right? Every day low prices, that sort of stuff. And you know, they like your point, they did flag higher gas. Now, we have a situation the stock's down 15%. It had gapped from those all-time highs after that report. They gave an a cautious outlook for the balance of the year again citing, you know, higher oil prices, that sort of thing. Do you think into the print expectations are too low and sentiment is not particularly great and therefore the stock could set up for a bounce especially as we've seen and I know, you know, the hyperscalers have had a big ramp over the last two weeks or so during that earning season, but you know, does Walmart look a lot like Amazon? You know, Walmart had 26% year-over-year e-commerce growth, right? They're taking more of the pie there and I'm just curious though if Walmart maybe becomes a bit more defensive on the way out of earnings. >> I I think it's going to be and I think you make a great point because we know a lot of a post-earning stock move has to do with what that stock did going into those earnings and in positioning. And it's trading at still an expensive multiple, but lower than than it than it was at the peak. You know, Walmart I put in the same bucket now in a sense with Procter & Gamble and Coke in the sense that it's the it's the anti-AI trade. So, the the days we're going to see a rest in AI uh trade stocks, we're going to uh I get a bounce in other things. It's like this constant either/or market. You're either buying hyper scale or selling semis. You're either selling semis and buying defensive. Uh this constant rotation that maybe yeah, you're making a great point that maybe the positioning could set Wal-Walmart up for a bounce. But, you know, one of the things that I want to hear is is we get a lot a lot of questions to retail CEOs during calls is what are you seeing within your income cohort? And I'm, you know, the the information that these retailers and restaurants gather is really tremendous in in in the sense of being able to gather uh that that sort of stratification of of income spending. And I want to hear, you know, it was some of the banking executives. Was it Moynihan or somebody else that oh, the K-shape is no longer applicable. And that lower income And then, you had the Kraft CEO said, I don't know about that. I'm I'm still seeing a K-shaped economy. Well, you know, I I I don't know if if Walmart's going to get into the into the letter game, but uh I I want to hear whether they use the word choiceful again. Because choiceful is not even in the Webster's dictionary. But, I think maybe it was the Walmart CFO that started using the word choiceful last last year. And I want to see and hear if he uses that word choiceful again. >> Well, you know what, Peter? What's not choiceful is what we need to do seemingly on a weekly basis. That's fill our cars up with gasoline. And you just mentioned the prices the fact that prices at this time of the year typically trending lower and they're not. So, I bring you to these energy stocks. As we're sitting here right now, what I find to be a well, not amazing cuz we've talked about this, but I think it would surprise people despite the fact that crude oil has come off significantly since the highs we saw four or five months ago. XLE is making a new all-time high. OIH has had a remarkable bounce off the 200-day moving average. These refining stocks continue to be on fire, no pun intended. So, energy is still sort of a place regardless of what's going on with semis and AI and and DRAM energy works. >> Refineries are seeing earnings growth as fast as the semis. And and I also think that from an energy investor perspective, at least on the crude side, and I put myself in this bucket since we're long then, is the belief that each day that passes, and of course you could have said this two to three months ago, without uh more than 100 ships going through the street, that we're just building up to this slow slow slow slow, no one cares, no one cares, and then all of a sudden this spike. And I go back to what uh Saudi Aramco said, I think it was either last week or the week before, talking about the dramatic drawdown in commercial inventories and strategic reserves that have been able to offset this major supply disruption. But, that lever, that inventory release, is sort of running out of steam. And you see that in the US level of SPRs, and they think we're just getting closer and closer to you can no longer sort of tap these extra inventories, and we're reaching a point where uh we're going to have a problem. And even if the war ended today, it would take 18 months of about 2 million barrels a day of extra inventory just to get back to where you were before the war started. In addition, what we're seeing is that energy is basically that safety trade. It is that geopolitical safety trade. Maybe, you know, it used to be gold, for example. Oh, you got to buy gold. Now, it's energy stocks. And I do think from a fundamental supply-demand perspective, you still need to be long them. And from a hedge perspective, I think it's a great sector to own. And it's still only about 3% of the S&P, which is which is unbelievable as well, very depressed. >> It is interesting to me, and guys brought this up on many occasions, that large integrateds have acted much better on the way down when crude got hit after the first MOU. It showed pretty good relative strength relative to obviously the the commodity. OIH got a bit harder hit, and it's a bit further from those prior highs than XLE is, but it seems like that is the sort of trade to everything that you just said, that makes sense. If you're going to have this premium built into crude, a geopolitical one, even if we have some sort of agreement anytime soon. Like your point, it just doesn't feel like we're going to see a whole host of traffic through the strait, but also, you know, the infrastructure rebuild. There's like been a lot of damage, right? And it's not just as far as crude, but LNG and the like. So, again, that'll be one to kind of keep a close eye on, especially >> And then also, to add to that, all the refilling of those drawn inventories >> Yeah. >> on top with natural demand. >> Yeah. >> So, there the the oil service stocks, and we own SLB, uh they're going to see great business over the next couple of years on that restocking story. >> Well, just bring it back to the AI thing and and taking it overseas. You know, you and I have had a couple great conversations with Louis Gave from Gave Kal over the last year or so, and one of the things that he seems fairly emphatic on is that, you know, whatever you think, you know, this this gap between US models and the Chinese models is closing pretty quickly. He's made the point to us on many of occasions that they have the lowest cost of capital, of labor, of energy, right? They have the support in many ways of the government. It is a matter of national security. We're starting to hear that a little bit more with our companies and maybe that's something that brings you back to that deal that we saw between the alternative lenders and Nvidia, right? And maybe it is the sort of thing where the government's like, "Listen, here's your backstop. We're not going to be the two big to fail guys, you know me swooping in." But when I think about Alibaba and Baidu, they report this week. Last time Alibaba reported, you ready for what their CapEx number was for the next 3 years? This is fiscal '26, '27, '28. $56 billion. Just think about that. And we've had our hyperscalers come out giving numbers, you know, Amazon's a great example. You know, coming into the year, their CapEx was $100 billion. Now it's up like 60% year-over-year. Now the pace in which the raises are going to, you know, start to decelerate to some degree. But if you think about the hundreds of billions each of these companies are spending, the trillions of dollars collectively, and their national champions are spending, you know, 56 billion. And you could say, "All right, fine, the government's subsidizing." So call it 100 billion. You know what I mean? It doesn't matter. Like, where does that put us from, you know, a capital standpoint, a debt standpoint? We see what's going on there relative to what's going on there. Cuz if they do close the gap, then you have to look at us and say, "Well, what the hell's going on here? Why have we done this to the tune of trillions of dollars?" >> To me, this is the biggest story over the next couple years is that these US models are now in a price war with China. You can be sure whenever this was, when Anthropic and OpenAI came out with their initial PowerPoint slide deck saying, "Hey, we're going to develop these models and we're going to charge a subscription fee and these are going to be our revenues over the next number of years, and they're obviously coming out with some revenue numbers ahead of their IPOs, and obviously business is growing fast. But, there was no realization and anticipation that the Chinese would end up being their biggest competitors. And in fact, to the point where the Chinese are almost going to give these models away for free. And no one's going to want to pay for your subscription at OpenAI and Anthropic unless you're a coder or you're a high-end enterprise user. So, that is massively disruptive to the entire business models of those two companies. And we know those two companies, or at least half or more of the backlogs of all the cloud companies. And and I've argued this for a while that OpenAI from that perspective in particular is too big to fail. Not they're going to get bailed out by the government, but because their tentacles have reached so far, and and Nvidia's are now reaching for two, and they're all obviously in bed together, that if OpenAI eventually can't make any money, and people are realizing that I'm not going to continue to sink a hundred billion dollars every time they want to fundraise, because I don't see a profitability light at the end of this tunnel, then this whole ecosystem gets massively disrupted. And I think that that's that appreciation is not fully felt. I think people are beginning to realize that yeah, we do need to compete against the Chinese, but you know, then then we react for maybe a week, and then it's back to buy buy the US AI tech trade. But, those Chinese companies haven't gone away, and they're only getting better. >> Yeah, no doubt about it. And and again, you're going to have a lot of technical folks and a lot of papers being written that their open-source or their open-weight models don't really kind of stack up to, you know, our best models here in the way that we are innovating, you know, using the best technology. But, when you think about the revenue that these companies are doing, it just came out this morning that OpenAI is on a $40 billion revenue run rate. And Anthropic is going to do, you ready for this? $100 to $120 billion in sales. Now, they're targeting a $2 trillion IPO maybe at some time in October. Now, OpenAI is not going to be, you know, too far behind that. But, these companies, the revenue ramps, this is not usually what we see from IPOs. Usually, we see, you know, the sort of a ramp coming over the next couple of years, and that's one of the reasons why you are interested in buying into an IPO. If you're Anthropic and you're going to come in and you're doing a $100 billion, right? But, then you start seeing decelerating growth because of all the competitive situation, these IPOs might end up being a flop. And that might be the reason, at least over the last few months, of what we've seen out of SpaceX because, yes, they are growing their sales fairly dramatically, you know, 100% year-over-year. It's supposed to go from 45 this year to 100 or so next, but these are very unprofitable companies. >> Ex- That's exactly right. We're we're we're in the ramp of revenue phase because a lot of them are selling into a lot of the U- US customers. Probably some European ones as well. That But, now you're beginning to them realize that maybe they priced it too much. I mean, OpenAI is talking about price cuts. And it's even on these revenue run rates is can it be a profitable business model at the end of the day? Is the level of CapEx that's embedded in these businesses going forward going to be good enough to provide uh that profit at the end of the day? So, we again, we're all talking about revenue numbers, and it's hugely impressive. But, is the rate of growth sustainable again when, you know, the average Chinese companies offering it for free? [snorts] You know, I I I I question that cuz free is pretty competitive, especially with the models that are so good. And just the the level and I keep going back to this, the level of maintenance CapEx, the level of cost structure that you're embedded in this business just to generate this this massive revenue spend is what is going to be the levelized profit margin for OpenAI and Anthropic. I don't know yet, but it's not going to be like the 85% old-school software business that Microsoft experienced for a while and Oracle and so forth. To me, it's going to be much lower. And what do you pay for that? Exciting technology for the rest for the rest of us, but what do you pay for a reduced profit margin relative to what was old-school tech, which was more asset light? >> Peter, let's go to my favorite fast slow-motion train wreck that is quickly becoming a fast-motion train wreck. That's obviously what's going on in Japan. Scott Bessent obviously has acknowledged there's a problem. Good for him because at least he's clever enough to see it. Intervention week and a half or 2 weeks ago between United States and the Bank of Japan, it worked, but it's not really working now. Bank of Japan's going to have to raise rates. It's just that simple. And I don't know what happens if and when. >> So, what was interesting about the the intervention when the US got involved was on the day of the BOJ meeting. The BOJ meeting was that night US time, and I immediately thought, well, in order to make this sustainable, you would assume that the Bank of Japan would follow through with a with a hike. Of course, they didn't. But, Ueda, Governor Ueda, did talk tough. And subsequent to that, we had, you know, the the news that Bessent was involved in terms of selling euro, buying yen, and utilizing this Fed facility, which technically hasn't actually been used yet by the Japanese. But, and then we had even tougher talk from the Bank of Japan. And what was most interesting this week was Prime Minister Takaichi is officially well, I should say unofficially cuz it was leaked through Bloomberg endorsing a BOJ hike. Cuz she now realizes that in order to sustain the yen rally, it's not just going to be intervention. That never lasts. It must be followed through with a rate increase. And it looks like September we're going to get it. Prior to the intervention, uh the swaps market was pricing in about a 25% chance that they would hike in September. And now that that uh those odds are about 75 to 80%. So, I do think that they're going to deliver. Then the question is is okay, what does that mean for the rest of the Japanese yield curve, the JGB yield curve? Does that temper the rise in long-term interest rates cuz now the BOJ is getting more serious about inflation? Well, a lot will depend if there's further follow-through and maybe a hike subsequent to the September hike. Uh and what does that mean for fund flows? At what level of JGB yield do Japanese investors say, "Hey, I can just keep my money home. I can get a really nice return. I'm going to take my money that's parked overseas and bring it back." And every time we get a rate move up, whether it's on the short end or it's the long end of the yield curve, we're getting closer to that repatriation story. >> Well, Peter Boockvar, we've gotten a lot of great feedback as you and Guy have been covering the situation with the dollar-yen. So, we appreciate you spending the time with us here on all of these topics. This is Peter Boockvar. He's the CIO of 1. BFG Wealth Partners. Thanks so much, Peter, for being with us again. >> Thank you, guys. >> This podcast is for informational purposes only. All opinions expressed by me, Dan Nathan, Guy Adami, and any other participants are solely our opinions and should not be relied upon for specific investment decisions.
